name: Turning Points and Eras
description: Fifty whole stories from the long middle of history: the purchases and partitions that moved whole territories on paper, the crusades taken one at a time, the treaties and settlements that closed a war, the revolutions and revolts, the expeditions by sea and overland, the plagues, the superstitions and market manias, and the ages and renaissances. Each subject carries twenty chapters that follow it in order, written in a calm even register for long listening, and each chapter says plainly what kind of record it rests on.

exclusions: No invented quotations, invented private thoughts, invented letters, invented dialogue or invented scenes; describe only what the record supports and say plainly where it stops.
No living people and nobody within living memory: every subject here is closed, and no descendant, claimant or present-day public figure is named or characterised.
No verdict passed on any person or party as hero or villain, no moralising, and no direct address urging the listener to think or do anything.
No modern political analogy, no claim about a present-day state, people, religion, party or border, and no partisan framing of a contested national history.
No hooks, cliffhangers, countdowns, teasers or alarm of any kind, at the opening of a chapter or anywhere inside it.
No dwelling on torture, execution, massacre, battlefield injury or sexual violence; state briefly that it happened and give the consequence, the settlement or the record the time instead.
Keep every chapter self-contained and resolving to a quiet close, with no reference forward to a later chapter and no callback to an earlier one.
No dates, casualty figures, prices or population numbers stated more precisely than the evidence allows, and no source cited by title, author, archive or shelfmark.
No mockery of anybody who held a belief described here, and no framing of any past explanation as stupid rather than as the reasoning available at the time.
No third-party retellings, films, games, novels or dramatisations; where a familiar version comes from a later invention, say so from the documentary record rather than from the retelling.
prompt_context: Each episode tells one turning point or one era entire, and each chapter is one stage of it told from beginning to quiet end. Name what happens in the chapter plainly in the first sentence: the chapter titles are the story in order, so a listener who wakes in the middle always knows where they are. Tell what happened and how it is known, and nothing else. No verdict is passed on anybody in these stories — no hero, no monster, no lesson drawn for the listener, and no comparison with any present-day country, party, government or dispute. Real historical figures are named plainly and described from the record; nobody living and nobody within living memory is named, and no invented quotation, invented letter, invented conversation or invented scene appears anywhere. Where the record stops, say so and stop with it. Say where each chapter's evidence comes from: the kind of document, the kind of object, the kind of excavation, the kind of measurement. Describe record types rather than naming a title, an author or an archive reference, and where two sources disagree, give both and leave the disagreement standing rather than smoothing it into one version. Several of these subjects are famous mainly through retellings that the archives do not support; when that is so, say plainly what the documents contain and how much of the familiar story rests on later invention, without mockery of anybody who believed it. Violence, famine, epidemic and forced labour appear in many of these stories. State what happened in one plain sentence and give the consequence, the settlement, the object or the transmission the time instead; no dwelling on injury, execution, torture or suffering, and no scene built for effect. This is a sleep compilation before it is anything else, so keep the tempo even and low the whole way through and let the detail carry it — the wording of a clause, the weight of a bulb, the length of a league, the number of days in a quarantine, the season a pass was crossed. Invent nothing. End each chapter on something still: a treaty printed, a boundary walked, a building left unfinished, a name that survives on a map.

the people who were not consulted, and the silence that leaves in the record
the afterlife, and what survives of the stage now in a law, a name or a border

the stage, then the variant account, then what both accounts agree on

evidence_expectations: Ground each stage in the kind of record named by the slot, and describe record types rather than citing any specific title, author, archive or shelfmark.
Say in every chapter whether the stage rests on a document, on an object, on an excavation, on a measurement or on a later retelling, and never let those blur together.
Where a stage survives in two accounts that disagree, give both and say they disagree, rather than choosing one or blending them.
Distinguish what a document says from what was actually done, and say plainly when a route, a boundary, a figure or a cause has been proposed but not established.
State the transmission honestly: how late the surviving copy is, who wrote it, what interest they had in the outcome, and what was lost or destroyed.
Give numbers as the evidence gives them: say when a figure is a count, when it is an estimate, and when the famous number has no surviving basis at all.
compatibility_rules: Pair only with the sleep history compilation formula; this pack assumes long, even chapters with no tension carried between them and no build across the episode.
Use one subject per episode and never mix two, so an episode is one turning point or one era told whole rather than an anthology.
Draw the twenty slots of a subject in order rather than at random, because the slots are the story in sequence and shuffling them breaks the promise the episode makes.
Never reuse a slot within one episode set; each slot is one stage of one story and a repeat would tell the same stage twice.
Do not pair with any formula that opens on a hook, builds tension, promises a revelation, or ends a chapter pointing forward; the exclusions forbid all four and the material does not need them.
